steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid import statement that imports both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs some adjustment. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react' using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App with proper TypeScript typing. The component should return a simple JSX element (like a div) for now.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to add a return type annotation (like : JSX.Element) for TypeScript.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create your App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named App is created with TypeScript typing and returns a JSX element.
successCriteria: Component named App exists
Component is a function
Component has a return type annotation (JSX.Element)
Component returns JSX
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the main App component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your component is named 'App', has a return type annotation (like : JSX.Element), and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined a function named 'App' with TypeScript typing that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize accessToken state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'accessToken' initialized as an empty string.
steps.hint: Remember to call useState with an initial value of '' and destructure the returned array into the state variable and setter function.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create your App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your App component will have an accessToken state variable ready to store the current access token value.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that creates an 'accessToken' state variable initialized as an empty string, with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the accessToken state variable. This will allow your component to track and update the current access token.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there's something missing. Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'accessToken' with an initial value of an empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look quite right. You need to use the useState hook inside your App component to create a state variable named 'accessToken' initialized as an empty string.

steps.title: Initialize refreshToken state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, add another useState hook to create a refreshToken state variable. Initialize it as an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the same useState pattern you used for accessToken, but name the variable refreshToken and set its initial value to ''.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a second state variable
const [refreshToken, setRefreshToken] = useState<string>('');
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create your App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component should now have two state variables: accessToken and refreshToken, both initialized as empty strings.
successCriteria: The code must include a refreshToken state variable declared with useState, initialized as an empty string, and placed inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a refreshToken state variable. This will store the refresh token needed for secure token rotation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that refreshToken is properly declared with useState and initialized as an empty string inside the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just adding the refreshToken state. Use useState with an empty string initial value, similar to how you created accessToken.

steps.title: Initialize tokenExpiry state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable named tokenExpiry. Initialize it with null.
steps.hint: Add a new useState call after your existing refreshToken state. Remember to use TypeScript's generic syntax to specify the type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a state variable with null
const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState<boolean | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a tokenExpiry state variable initialized to null, ready to track when your access token expires.
successCriteria: The code includes a useState call for tokenExpiry with null as initial value and proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the tokenExpiry state. This will help track when your access token needs to be refreshed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Used useState, 2) Named the variable tokenExpiry, 3) Initialized it with null, and 4) Added proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just initializing the tokenExpiry state. Use useState with null as the initial value, and make sure to include TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Define handleLogin function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named handleLogin that simulates a successful login by setting the accessToken, refreshToken, and tokenExpiry states with mock values.
steps.hint: Create an arrow function or regular function that calls the setter functions (setAccessToken, setRefreshToken, setTokenExpiry) with appropriate string values.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleLogin function that sets all three token-related state values when called.
successCriteria: The handleLogin function must be defined inside the App component and call setAccessToken, setRefreshToken, and setTokenExpiry with appropriate values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleLogin function that simulates token acquisition. This function will be used to initialize the token states.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but it doesn't set all three required state values. Make sure to call setAccessToken, setRefreshToken, and setTokenExpiry with appropriate values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleLogin function is not properly defined. It should be a function that sets the accessToken, refreshToken, and tokenExpiry states with mock values.

steps.title: Define handleRefresh function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named handleRefresh that will simulate refreshing the access token. This function should update the accessToken and tokenExpiry states using the refreshToken.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses the existing setAccessToken and setTokenExpiry functions to update state values. You can simulate a new token by generating a string.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleRefresh function is added to the component that updates accessToken and tokenExpiry state.
successCriteria: Function named handleRefresh is defined
Function calls setAccessToken with a new token value
Function calls setTokenExpiry with a new expiry timestamp
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleRefresh function. This function simulates refreshing the access token by updating both the accessToken and tokenExpiry states.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining the handleRefresh function, but it needs to properly update both accessToken and tokenExpiry states. Make sure your function calls setAccessToken and setTokenExpiry with appropriate values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleRefresh function is not properly defined. You need to create a function that updates both the accessToken and tokenExpiry states using their setter functions.

steps.title: Return the main container div
steps.instruction: In your App component, return a div element with a className of 'app'.
steps.hint: Replace the existing return statement with a div that has the className attribute set to 'app'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div element with className='app' as its root container.
successCriteria: The component returns JSX
The JSX contains a div element
The div has a className attribute
The className value is 'app'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully set up the main container with the correct className. This provides a CSS hook for styling the entire app.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your div element has exactly className='app' (not class or something else).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div with className='app'. Make sure you're returning JSX with the correct attribute.

steps.title: Add token display section
steps.instruction: Inside the main container div, add a section that displays the current accessToken, refreshToken, and tokenExpiry values.
steps.hint: Create a <div> or <section> element with appropriate headings and paragraphs to show each token value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of displaying state values in JSX

Current Tokens

Access Token: {accessToken}

Refresh Token: {refreshToken}

Token Expiry: {tokenExpiry}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a visible section showing the current token values (initially null).
successCriteria: Contains JSX element(s) inside the main div
Displays accessToken value
Displays refreshToken value
Displays tokenExpiry value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a section to display all three token values. This allows users to see the current authentication state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some display elements, but make sure you're showing all three token values (accessToken, refreshToken, and tokenExpiry) inside the main container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The token display section is missing or incomplete. Add a section inside the main div that shows the current values of accessToken, refreshToken, and tokenExpiry.

steps.title: Add login button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a <button> element with the text 'Login' and wire its onClick event to call the handleLogin function.
steps.hint: Remember to use the onClick prop and pass the handleLogin function reference (not call it immediately).
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Login' appears in the UI, and clicking it will trigger the handleLogin function when it's defined.
successCriteria: Button element with text 'Login'
onClick prop set to handleLogin
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a login button and wired it to the handleLogin function. The button will trigger token acquisition when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have both: a button with the text 'Login' and its onClick prop set to handleLogin (not handleLogin()).
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a button element with the text 'Login' and connect its onClick event to the handleLogin function.

steps.title: Add refresh button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Refresh Token' inside your component's return statement. Wire its onClick event to call the handleRefresh function.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element with text content and an onClick handler that references your existing handleRefresh function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button with onClick handler
<button onClick={handleRefresh}>Refresh Token</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Refresh Token' appears in the UI that will trigger the handleRefresh function when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element with text 'Refresh Token'
onClick handler set to handleRefresh function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a refresh button that will call the handleRefresh function when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both the button with 'Refresh Token' text and the onClick handler wired to handleRefresh.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Check that you have a <button> element with 'Refresh Token' text and onClick={handleRefresh}.

steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element below the token display section that explains the concept of secure token rotation and why it's important.
steps.hint:
Add a

Secure token rotation helps protect against token theft by regularly issuing new access tokens while using refresh tokens to maintain user sessions without requiring re-authentication.
steps.expectedOutcome: The app will now include educational text explaining secure token rotation concepts to users.

Include text about secure token rotation
